subject: Opendoor pilot — throughput & latency qualification follow-up
messages:
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi@redwood.com>
To: Mike Torres <mike@opendoor.ai>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 22 Mar 2028 15:10:00 -0700
Subject: Opendoor pilot — throughput & latency qualification follow-up

Hi Mike — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can size the pilot correctly. Please correct anything I got wrong.

Call highlights:
- Target UX SLO: p95 end-to-end response <= 250ms for single-turn paraphrase/normalize calls (these are the most latency-sensitive).
- Typical request mix: 70% short normalization prompts (~30–80 tokens), 25% mid-length transforms (~200–600 tokens), 5% long analysis (~1.5k+ tokens) used for nightly jobs.
- Burst profile: expected spikes during ETL jobs and product syncs — worst bursts observed historically ~300 QPS sustained for ~45s, with isolated peaks up to ~900 QPS for <10s during rollouts.
- Concurrency requirement: client wants ability to run 150 concurrent streaming sessions (chunked responses) with sub-500ms token-to-token latency.
- Acceptable fallback: if prod model cannot meet p95, degrade to cached short-responses or a cheaper quantized variant for non-critical routes.

Questions / clarifications we need from Opendoor (action: Mike):
1) Can you share a 24-hour token distribution sample (tokens/sec per minute) for recent production traffic? CSV or sample traces are fine.
2) For streaming routes, are clients doing immediate-render (each token streamed to user) or batching on the client side? That changes our minimum per-session throughput requirement.
3) Any hard constraints on cold-start latency when a new worker is spun up?

Suggested Redwood pilot plan (action: Naomi/Rishi):
- Stage 1 (lab): model/quantization profile test with representative token mix; we’ll run synthetic bursts to validate p95 and sustained qps.
- Stage 2 (canary): route 10% of traffic to pilot capacity with monitoring for p95, error rate, and token cost delta.
- Stage 3 (scale): scale to target sustained QPS and validate streaming token-latency at 150 concurrent sessions.

Attachments: I’ve attached a quick token profile template (opendoor_token_profile_v1.csv) and a short pilot runbook (pilot_runbook_v0.2.pdf) that outlines our test harness and KPIs.

Next steps / timelines:
- Mike to send token sample by Mon 26 Mar.
- We’ll turn around initial lab numbers within 3 business days after we receive the sample.

Thanks —

Thanks Naomi — great summary. Confirming the main points and answering your questions inline.

1) Token sample: attaching a 24h export (trimmed) — shows a baseline of ~40 QPS with nightly batch windows that hit ~280 QPS for ~40–50s. The 900 QPS spikes are from CI/rollout tests we run occasionally; they’re synthetic but representative of what we might see on day 0.
2) Streaming: clients do immediate-render; they render token-by-token in the UX. So per-token latency matters for perceived responsiveness.
3) Cold starts: we can tolerate ~1.5s cold-start for non-streaming routes, but streaming sessions need warm workers (prefer zero cold-start for streaming routes).

We’re attaching the token export and a short doc on client rendering behavior. Let us know if you need additional fields.

Naomi / team — quick technical note after eyeballing the sample Mike sent.

Preliminary observations:
- The token mix looks skewed toward short requests (50–75 tokens) as discussed; this favors batching but the streaming immediate-render constraint kills aggressive batching on those routes.
- For the streaming sessions: we should treat them as low-latency preference flows — configure small continuous batches (1–4 tokens) and dedicate a warm pool for streaming so cold-starts are avoided.
- Burst mitigation: KV prefix caching will cut cost and latency for repeated prompts. Recommend enabling prefix caching and a 60s in-memory TTL for the pilot.

Sizing estimate (very rough, lab-level):
- Steady-state (baseline 40 QPS): single p4d-style pool with 4 cards (quantized model variant) should be comfortable and hit p95 < 200ms for short prompts.
- Burst headroom: to sustain 300 QPS for 45s with p95 < 250ms, we’ll need autoscale that can spin additional capacity up to ~14 GPUs (depends on model variant/quantization).
- Peak 900 QPS (10s): treat as exceptional; fallback route => non-streaming cached responses or queueing with throttled UX degrade.

Questions for sizing precision (action: Priyom):
- Priyom, can you run a quick sim using the attached CSV and our default gpt-mini quant profiles and capture tokens/sec and per-token latency at different batch sizes? If you can get that by EOD tomorrow, we’ll convert this into a pilot capacity table.

Rishi

Quick simulation result (attached small report) — ran the CSV through gpt-mini quantized profile with continuous batching sizes {1,2,4,8}. High-level:
- Batch size 1 (stream-friendly): median per-token latency 18ms, p95 token latency 48ms. Sustained throughput per GPU ~420 tokens/sec for short prompts.
- Batch size 4: median 26ms, p95 72ms, throughput ~930 tokens/sec per GPU. Good for non-streaming mid-length jobs.
- At baseline 40 QPS (short prompts), a single GPU gives ~4–5x headroom; to hit 300 QPS we recommend 6 GPUs with warm streaming pool of 2 GPUs dedicated to streaming sessions to keep cold-starts at zero.

Attached: sim_summary_opendoor_v1.pdf and a quick runbook snippet with recommended autoscale policy. I’ll add a capacity table (GPUs vs QPS vs expected p95) to the shared Drive link tomorrow.
